name: Kugu Nganhcara

catalog_locator: Verstraete 2021, sec. 3.3 'Diachronic implications', author-manuscript p. 17 (saved text the copy we hold; (15a) on MS p. 19; published pp. 152-173. Blevins 2025: printed p. 142 (held at, text).
catalog_quote: There are three indications that the original stress system in Umpithamu must have been one that was left-aligned, with a leftmost stress rule. The first indication is local, relating to Umpithamu’s closest relatives. Most other Middle Paman languages for which we have a reliable description of word stress have a system of this kind: this is the case, for instance, in Wik Mungkan (Kilham 1974), Kugu Nganhcara (Smith & Johnson 2000), Wik Ngathan (Sutton 1978) and possibly also Umpila (Thompson 1988).5 [fn. 5: There are some complications in Umpila relating to syllable weight (due to the occurrence of vowel length beyond the first syllable).] ... (15) Starting point a. Stress: Left-to-right parsing, leftmost stress rule ... [Blevins 2025: 142, same primary:] One of these is Kugu Nganhcara, a Pama-Nyungan language of Australia, as described by Smith & Johnson (2000). In this language, with consonants /p, t, t̪, c, k, b, d, d̪, j, g, m, n, n̪, ɲ, ŋ, l, r, w, j/, all consonants except the tap, /r/, have geminate allophones optionally in intervocalic position following a short initial stressed syllable.

The surrounding section restates the same as (15a) p.19 'S…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand: Kugu Nganhcara (the patrilect cluster that includes Kugu Mu'inh) is reported, on the authority of Smith & Johnson 2000, to have a left-aligned system with primary stress assigned by a leftmost rule, i.e. on the word-initial syllable. The only first-hand prosodic remark reachable (Smith 1986: 517, on the sister patrilect Kugu Muminh, seen via IA search snippets) says the language 'is a syllable-timed language, though initial syllables are about 20% longer than comparable non-initial syllables', contrasting it with Wik Munkan where 'initial syllables are rhythmically strong (i.e. stressed)' -- so initial prominence in Nganhcara is weak/durational rather than a strong dynamic stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing specific to Kugu Nganhcara; Verstraete notes only the general Pama-Nyungan reports of alternating secondary stress (and the 'stress ghosting' caveat).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Kugu Nganhcara. Smith & Johnson 1986 note vowel length is generally restricted to initial syllables (consistent with initial prominence); Smith 1986 and Evans 1995 characterise the language as syllable-timed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level typological summary by a third party; the primary statement (Smith & Johnson 2000, HAL vol. 5) was not seen, so the exact formulation, domain (root vs word, treatment of enclitics, compounds) and any caveat about weak stress remain unverified.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements found refer to Kugu Nganhcara as a whole (Glottolog cover languoid wikn1246 'Wikngenchera'; WALS knc), the cluster of six or seven mutually intelligible patrilects of which Kuku-Mu'inh (kuku1282, xmp) is one; Smith & Johnson 1986 say the patrilects 'differ in only minor aspects of their morphology and phonology' (Mu'inh-specific: alveolars realised as retroflexes). The one first-hand prosodic remark (Smith 1986) is specifically about the sister patrilect Kugu Muminh (kuku1283, xmh) as spoken at Edward River. No source seen describes Mu'inh prosody separately.

new_statements.quote: As for whether there are languages (outside Austronesian) with tonic gemination after all vowels, the answer appears to be yes. One of these is Kugu Nganhcara, a Pama-Nyungan language of Australia, as described by Smith & Johnson (2000). In this language, with consonants /p, t, t̪, c, k, b, d, d̪, j, g, m, n, n̪, ɲ, ŋ, l, r, w, j/, all consonants except the tap, /r/, have geminate allophones optionally in intervocalic position following a short initial stressed syllable.

The quoted sentences are there word for word: 'As for whether there are languages (outside Austronesian) with tonic gemination after all vowels, the answer appears to be yes. One of these is Kugu Nganhcara, a Pama-Nyungan language of Australia, as described by Smith & Johnson (2000). In this language, with consonants /p, t, t̪, c, k, b, d, d̪, j, g, m, n, n̪, ɲ, ŋ,…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (initial-syllable stress, initial stress) and as the existing Verstraete 2021 statement that Kugu Nganhcara (Smith & Johnson 2000) has a left-aligned, leftmost-stress system. Second-hand: Blevins reports Smith & Johnson (2000), the primary description, which is still unseen (print-only Handbook of Australian Languages vol. 5). Not a stress description: one sentence in a chapter about Austronesian sound change, and stress is mentioned only as the environment of allophonic gemination. Blevins cites Smith & Johnson 2000 as pp. 357-507 whereas the kuku1282 record has 355-489; a citation discrepancy only.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is presupposed to fall on the initial syllable: the geminate allophones of consonants occur intervocalically after a short initial stressed syllable. The chapter states no stress rule of its own for Kugu Nganhcara; it reports the gemination environment from Smith & Johnson (2000) and takes initial stress as given.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. The gemination is optional and excludes the tap /r/; the stressed initial syllable in the environment is a short one (long vowels are elsewhere reported as restricted to initial syllables, so the 'short' condition concerns vowel length, not stress placement).
new_statements.identity_note: Blevins names the language 'Kugu Nganhcara' as a whole, following Smith & Johnson (2000), and does not specify a patrilect (Mu'inh, Muminh, Uwanh, Ugbanh, Yi'anh, Mangk). The kuku1282 record header treats the item as Kuku-Mu'inh (ISO xmp), one of the Kugu Nganhcara patrilects; the reported stress facts are for the Nganhcara group generally.
